title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
Bottom line. Bender’s most-used word is his own name (206 times), then “fry” (158). “Ass” is only his 7th most-used word, but he says it 67 times, more than anyone else in the show.
In “War Is the H-Word,” the plot turns on a bomb that will go off when Bender says his most-used word. Fans have always assumed they know what that word is. I counted every word Bender says across all 140 episodes to check.

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
section: His top word is his own name
text:
His top word is his own name
Bender talks about Bender a lot. After removing common words like “the” and “I,” and filler like “hey” and “yeah,” his own name tops the list, followed by his best friend’s.


Show code
plot_top <- function(mode) {
  top_words |>
    filter(rank <= 15) |>
    slice_head(n = 15) |>
    mutate(word = fct_reorder(word, n), is_ass = word == "ass") |>
    ggplot(aes(n, word, fill = is_ass)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.72) +
    geom_text(aes(label = n, fontface = ifelse(is_ass, "bold", "plain")),
              hjust = -0.25, size = 3.6, colour = label_ink(mode)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pe_green, `TRUE` = focus)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
    labs(x = "Times said", y = NULL) +
    theme_pe(mode)
}
plot_top("light")
plot_top("dark")




Bender’s 15 most-used words







Bender’s 15 most-used words





Ties share a rank, so “god” and “guys” are both 9th. Stemming, which folds “asses” into “ass” but also merges other words’ variants, drops “ass” to 10th.

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
Nobody says “ass” more
He may not say it most often, but he says it more than anyone else, and it isn’t close. Fry is a distant second with 14.

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
Per word spoken, it’s closer
Bender also talks more than almost anyone, so raw counts flatter him. Scaling by how much each character says changes the picture: among characters with at least 2,000 words, Mom says “ass” at a slightly higher rate. That rests on just 5 uses, though, so I wouldn’t put much weight on it.


Show code
rate_data <- totals |>
  filter(words >= 2000) |>
  left_join(select(ass_users, speaker, ass_exact), by = "speaker") |>
  filter(coalesce(ass_exact, 0) > 0) |>   # characters who say it at least once
  mutate(
         rate = 1e4 * ass_exact / words,
         speaker = fct_reorder(speaker, rate),
         is_bender = speaker == "Bender")

plot_rate <- function(mode) {
  ggplot(rate_data, aes(rate, speaker, colour = is_bender)) +
    geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = rate, yend = speaker), linewidth = 0.6, alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_point(size = 3.2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(ass_exact, ifelse(ass_exact == 1, " use", " uses"))), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.3,
              colour = if (mode == "light") "#5f6670" else "#aab1ba") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = pe_green, `TRUE` = focus)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
    labs(x = "Per 10,000 words spoken", y = NULL) +
    theme_pe(mode)
}
plot_rate("light")
plot_rate("dark")

title: What Is Bender’s Most-Used Word?
text:
How this was done






NoteMethods and limitations





Data. Transcripts of all 140 broadcast episodes from The Infosphere, collected in 2023. The 140 include the four films, which aired as 16 “Part” episodes. Only aggregated counts are published here; the transcripts and scraping code are not.
Cleaning. Most transcript pages had never been split into speaker and line, so I re-split every line on its first colon. That kept 1,010 lines that contain a second colon, which my 2023 version cut off. Stage directions in brackets and parentheses are removed from both the speaker and the line. Alternate-universe, robot, and ghost versions of the main cast count as the same character. The result is 28,949 spoken lines.
Words. Tokenized with tidytext. Common words are removed using tidytext’s stop-word lists, plus interjections and filler (“hey,” “yeah,” “uh,” “gonna,” and stretched spellings like “ohhhh”). Stemming uses the Porter stemmer. Ties share a rank.
Why remove filler. With stop words alone, “hey” edges out “bender” as his top word:









Definition
Top five




Stop words and filler removed (used here)
bender (206), fry (158), robot (123), time (84), wait (83)


Stop words only
hey (212), bender (206), yeah (172), fry (158), robot (123)





What changed from 2023. The original version of this analysis (published on LinkedIn) counted “bender” 375 times. That was inflated: its cleaning removed parenthetical directions but left bracketed ones like “[Bender walks in]” in the dialogue.
Limitations. Two episodes are mostly missing from the source: “Naturama” is one unsplit block of text and “Saturday Morning Fun Pit” largely is too, so those blocks are left out. “Zapp Dingbat” and “Meanwhile” have short transcripts at the source. Fan transcripts also miss or mishear some lines.

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
text: Bottom line. Inclusion of all SNAP retailers in food access analysis leaves critical blind spots and substantially underestimates the number of people in food deserts.

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
text:
USDA changed the definition in 2026

Since 2011, the USDA has identified and mapped areas with low access to food, first as the Food Desert Locator and, from 2013, as the Food Access Research Atlas. The atlas has always asked the same question: how many people in a census tract live far from a store that sells a full range of groceries? Until this year, the types of stores were supermarkets, supercenters, or large grocery stores. Dollar stores, drug stores, and convenience stores were not part of the analysis.
In July 2026, USDA split the atlas in two:

The Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM) is the original atlas under a new name. It still counts only large grocery retailers and still runs on the 2019 store list and 2010 census tracts used in the 2021 edition of FARA.
The SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM) is new. It counts every store authorized to accept SNAP except farmers markets and delivery routes, using a 2025 store list and 2020 tracts. That includes dollar stores, chain pharmacies, and convenience stores, roughly 4 times as many stores nationwide (245,414 against 62,020 large grocery retailers in the current SNAP list).

USDA publishes both, and they give very different answers. But, because of the different vintages of data, comparing them directly can’t say how much of the difference comes from which stores count, because they also differ in store-list year, tract boundaries, and how they place people on the map. This analysis holds all of that fixed and changes only the store definition.

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
text:
How the measure works

Our key measure asks for every person in Pennsylvania, how far is the nearest store that counts? I identify that distance as a straight line census block by census block, then roll the answers up to census tracts, as the USDA indicates.


Show code
import inspect
import json
import warnings

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

# Street basemap: OpenStreetMap's standard tiles (no API key), fetched once when
# the page renders and toned to grey so the data stays in front. Needs
# contextily; without it, or offline, the figure renders without a basemap.
try:
    import contextily as cx
except ImportError:
    cx = None
    warnings.warn("contextily not installed: method figure renders without a basemap")
TILES = "https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png"
# OpenStreetMap blocks tile requests that don't identify the app making them
# ("Access blocked" tiles), so name this site instead of contextily's random ID.
TILE_HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "sean-hudson-portfolio/1.0 (+https://sean-hudson-data.github.io)",
                "Referer": "https://sean-hudson-data.github.io/"}
if cx is not None:
    cx.tile.USER_AGENT = TILE_HEADERS["User-Agent"]


def tone(img, mode):
    """Greyscale the tiles: pale for light mode, inverted and dim for dark."""
    rgb = img[..., :3].astype(float)
    grey = rgb @ np.array([0.299, 0.587, 0.114])
    grey = 255 - (255 - grey) * 0.45 if mode == "light" else 18 + (255 - grey) * 0.3
    out = img.copy()
    out[..., :3] = np.clip(grey, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)[..., None]
    return out

with open("data/pa_tracts.geojson") as f:
    tract_geom = next(feat["geometry"] for feat in json.load(f)["features"]
                      if feat["properties"]["tract_geoid"] == illus_tract_id)
outline = (tract_geom["coordinates"] if tract_geom["type"] == "MultiPolygon"
           else [tract_geom["coordinates"]])
lat0 = illus_blocks["lat"].mean()
panels = [("large", "Large grocery retailers only", illus_stores["large"]),
          ("all", "Every SNAP retailer", illus_stores["large"] | True)]


def add_tiles(ax, mode, ink):
    """Draw map tiles under everything; leave the axes untouched if that fails.

    Tiles cover a padded window, because matplotlib widens one axis at draw time
    to keep the map's aspect ratio."""
    (w, e), (south, n) = ax.get_xlim(), ax.get_ylim()
    pad_x, pad_y = (e - w) * 0.4, (n - south) * 0.4
    try:
        extra = ({"headers": TILE_HEADERS}
                 if "headers" in inspect.signature(cx.bounds2img).parameters else {})
        img, ext = cx.bounds2img(w - pad_x, south - pad_y, e + pad_x, n + pad_y, zoom=14,
                                 source=TILES, ll=True, **extra)
        img, ext = cx.warp_tiles(tone(img, mode), ext, t_crs="EPSG:4326")
    except Exception as err:  # offline, or the tile server refused
        warnings.warn(f"basemap skipped: {err}")
        return
    ax.imshow(img, extent=ext, zorder=0, interpolation="bilinear")
    ax.set_xlim(w, e)
    ax.set_ylim(south, n)
    ax.text(0.995, 0.005, "© OpenStreetMap contributors", transform=ax.transAxes,
            ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=6, color=ink, alpha=0.8, zorder=5)


def share_label(share):
    pct = "over 99%" if 0.99 < share < 1 else f"{share:.0%}"
    return f"{pct} of the outlined tract's residents live more than a mile away"


def method_chart(mode):
    ink = "#343a40" if mode == "light" else "#e3e6ea"
    near = "#2a78d6" if mode == "light" else "#3987e5"
    far = "#eb6834" if mode == "light" else "#d95926"
    line = "#9aa0a6" if mode == "light" else "#6b7280"
    edge = "white" if mode == "light" else "#212529"

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5.6), layout="constrained")
    fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
    for ax, (key, title, counts) in zip(axes, panels):
        ax.set_facecolor("none")
        ax.set_aspect(1 / np.cos(np.deg2rad(lat0)), adjustable="datalim")
        for _, r in illus_tract.iterrows():
            ax.plot([r["lon"], r[f"store_lon_{key}"]], [r["lat"], r[f"store_lat_{key}"]],
                    color=line, lw=0.6, alpha=0.7, zorder=1)
        beyond = illus_blocks[f"dist_{key}_m"] > METRES_PER_MILE
        ax.scatter(illus_blocks["lon"], illus_blocks["lat"],
                   s=np.sqrt(illus_blocks["pop"]) * 2.2, c=np.where(beyond, far, near),
                   alpha=0.8, linewidths=0, zorder=2)
        for poly in outline:
            x, y = zip(*poly[0])
            ax.plot(x, y, color=ink, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
        s = illus_stores.loc[counts]
        ax.scatter(s["lon"], s["lat"], marker="s", s=34, color=ink, edgecolors=edge,
                   linewidths=0.8, zorder=4)
        share = (illus_tract.loc[illus_tract[f"dist_{key}_m"] > METRES_PER_MILE, "pop"].sum()
                 / illus_tract["pop"].sum())
        ax.set_title(f"{title}\n{share_label(share)}", loc="left", color=ink, fontsize=10.5)
        ax.set_xlim(illus_blocks["lon"].min(), illus_blocks["lon"].max())
        ax.set_ylim(illus_blocks["lat"].min(), illus_blocks["lat"].max())
        ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_yticks([])
        for spine in ax.spines.values():
            spine.set_visible(False)
        # 1-mile scale bar
        dlon = METRES_PER_MILE / (111_320 * np.cos(np.deg2rad(lat0)))
        x0, y0 = illus_blocks["lon"].min() + 0.002, illus_blocks["lat"].min() + 0.002
        ax.plot([x0, x0 + dlon], [y0, y0], color=ink, lw=2, zorder=5)
        ax.text(x0 + dlon / 2, y0 + 0.0015, "1 mile", ha="center", color=ink, fontsize=9,
                zorder=5)
        if cx is not None:
            add_tiles(ax, mode, ink)
    handles = [
        Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=near, label="Block within 1 mile"),
        Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", color=far, label="Block more than 1 mile away"),
        Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", color=ink, label="Store that counts"),
        Line2D([], [], color=line, label="Line to nearest store"),
    ]
    fig.legend(handles=handles, loc="outside lower center", ncol=4, frameon=False,
               labelcolor=ink, fontsize=9)
    plt.show()

Each dot is a census block’s internal point, sized by population. Lines connect each block in the outlined tract to its nearest store.







Each dot is a census block’s internal point, sized by population. Lines connect each block in the outlined tract to its nearest store.






Step by step:

Start with people, where they live. The 2020 Census counts population for every census block, the smallest unit it publishes (336,985 blocks in Pennsylvania, many no bigger than a city block). Each block is represented by its internal point, a location the Census Bureau places inside the block.
Find the nearest store. For each block, the straight-line distance to the nearest store that counts, measured along the Earth’s surface. The search covers every store in the country, so a block near a state line can find a store across it.
Pick the threshold. USDA uses different distances for urban and rural tracts: 1 mile in urban tracts and 10 miles in rural ones (with ½-mile and 20-mile variants). The urban flag is USDA’s own, so the threshold for every tract matches theirs.
Count the people beyond it. Everyone in a block whose internal point is farther than the threshold counts as beyond it. Summing those blocks gives the number of people beyond the threshold in each tract, and dividing by the tract’s population gives the share.
Apply USDA’s rule. A tract is low access if at least 500 people, or at least a third of its residents, are beyond the threshold. It is low income, low access (the usual “food desert”) if it is also one of USDA’s low-income tracts.







NoteTwo numbers that both get called “people in food deserts”






People beyond the threshold: only the people who live farther than the threshold from a store. This is the number in step 4.
People in low-access tracts: everyone living in a tract that meets the rule, including neighbors who live next to a store. Headlines like “X million Americans live in food deserts” use this one, because the designation belongs to the tract.

The second is always larger. This page says which one it means each time.

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
text:
How USDA measures it

LRAM and SRAM also measure distance differently from each other, and from this page.

The Large Retailer Access Map (LRAM) is the original atlas. It spreads 2010 Census population evenly across half-kilometer grid squares and measures from each square to the nearest supermarket, supercenter, or large grocery store, using a 2019 store list and 2010 tract boundaries.
The SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (SRAM), released in July 2026, draws a circle of each threshold distance around every SNAP-authorized store (as of June 2025) and counts the people outside every circle, using LandScan USA’s roughly 90-meter population grid and 2020 tracts.

Both then apply the same low-access rule as step 5. A circle of a mile around every store and the distance to the nearest store are two views of the same thing: someone is outside every circle exactly when their nearest store is more than a mile away. So the three approaches differ mainly in where they put people and which stores they count.










This page
USDA LRAM (original atlas)
USDA SRAM




Where people are
2020 census block internal points
2010 Census, spread over 0.5 km grid squares
LandScan USA, ~90 m grid


Stores
SNAP Retailer Locator, August 2026; any combination of types
Large grocery retailers, 2019 list
All SNAP retailers except farmers markets, June 2025


Distance
Straight line to the nearest store
From each grid square to the nearest store

Can change which stores count?
Yes

This page uses straight-line distance throughout, because LRAM only measures straight-line distance and the point here is to change one thing at a time. But SRAM’s driving-distance version is a real improvement. Straight lines can only approximate the distance between places and will always underestimate it.. Measured by driving distance, SRAM flags 872 Pennsylvania tracts as low access instead of 491, and 103 as low income and low access instead of 31. Unfortunately this increase is partly hidden by the broader store definition: the two changes push in opposite directions, so the driving-distance count ends up not far from what large grocery stores alone would give, while describing something quite different.
Holding everything but the store list fixed is the point: it lets the ladder and map below isolate the definition, and “Does it reproduce USDA’s numbers?” checks the method against SRAM.

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
text:
Why the definition matters
Counting a store as food access assumes people can buy affordable, nutritious food there. That holds for a supermarket or grocery store. It often doesn’t for the stores the broader definition adds. Convenience stores charge more per item and carry few of the staples you’d need to cook healthy meals on a budget such as fresh produce, meat, whole grains. Dollar stores are cheaper but usually carry a narrow selection with unfavorable unit costs, and where they spread they can push out the grocery stores that did. A store that accepts SNAP down the street isn’t the same as convenient access to affordable, nutritious food, but the broader definition counts it that way.
The designation also decides where money goes. Grant programs, healthy food financing, and nonprofit planning use these low-access areas to decide where help is needed. Under the broader definition, Pennsylvania’s low-income, low-access tracts drop from 220 to 36, and 536,149 people in low-income tracts stop showing up, even though many of them still live more than a mile from a grocery store. If programs follow the new definition, those are the places that could fall off the map.

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
section: Adding stores one type at a time
text:
Adding stores one type at a time



Show code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

labels = main["label"].tolist()
panels = [("Low-access tracts", la), ("Low-income, low-access tracts", lila)]


def ladder_chart(mode):
    ink = "#343a40" if mode == "light" else "#e3e6ea"
    muted = "#5f6670" if mode == "light" else "#aab1ba"
    bar = "#2a78d6" if mode == "light" else "#3987e5"

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.6), sharey=True,
                             layout="constrained")
    fig.patch.set_alpha(0)
    for ax, (title, values) in zip(axes, panels):
        y = range(len(values))
        ax.barh(y, values.to_numpy(), color=bar, height=0.62)
        for yi, val in zip(y, values.to_numpy()):
            ax.text(val + values.max() * 0.02, yi, f"{val:,}", va="center",
                    color=ink, fontsize=10)
        ax.set_title(title, loc="left", color=ink, fontsize=11.5)
        ax.set_xlim(0, values.max() * 1.18)
        ax.set_facecolor("none")
        ax.tick_params(colors=muted, length=0)
        ax.set_xticks([])
        for side in ("top", "right", "bottom", "left"):
            ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    axes[0].set_yticks(range(len(labels)), labels, color=ink, fontsize=10)
    axes[0].invert_yaxis()  # shared y: inverting once flips both panels
    plt.show()


ladder_chart("light")




Pennsylvania census tracts flagged under each definition (1 mile urban, 10 miles rural)

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
text:
Does it reproduce USDA’s numbers?
LRAM still runs on 2010 tract boundaries and a 2019 store list, so it isn’t a fair benchmark. SRAM is: it uses current tracts and stores, and when this method counts the same stores SRAM does, the two should agree. They do. At the standard thresholds, they classify 97.6% of Pennsylvania tracts the same way. That figure partly reflects how few tracts are low access at all, so the stricter measure is kappa, which discounts agreement by chance: 0.90, conventionally “almost perfect.” The two still differ in where they place people (block points here, a fine population grid for USDA), so the numbers aren’t identical, but they’re close enough that differences across store definitions come from the definition, not the method.Most importantly, we don’t see disproportionate errors in combined low-income low-access tracts.

NoteHow much does the block approximation matter?





Everyone in a block gets the distance from the block’s internal point. That’s exact for small city blocks and rough for large rural ones. To bound it, a block counts as ambiguous when the threshold falls within its effective radius (the radius of a circle with the block’s land area), so part of it could sit on either side.
8% of Pennsylvanians live in ambiguous blocks under the large-grocery definition (6% with every SNAP retailer). Counting every ambiguous block as entirely inside, then entirely beyond, the threshold puts low-access tracts at 869–1,163 under the large-grocery definition and 356–651 with every SNAP retailer. These are worst cases, since a real block is rarely all on one side. Even at the extremes the ranges don’t overlap, so the gap between the two definitions is larger than anything the approximation could produce.

title: Which Stores Count? Food Desert Status Depends on the Definition
section: What this can and can’t say
text:
What this can and can’t say
Straight-line distance understates how far people actually travel, so every count here is conservative; USDA’s driving-distance figures flag considerably more tracts. Even so, the choice of stores matters more than the choice of distance: with straight-line distance, counting only large grocery stores puts 2.5 times as many Pennsylvanians beyond the threshold as counting every SNAP retailer.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
text: Bottom line. Adopting an MCO model does appear to reduce annual per-enrollee expenditures to IDD waiver services.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: Why states moved I/DD services into managed care
text:
Why states moved I/DD services into managed care

States moved I/DD services from fee-for-service into managed care for largely the same reasons they’ve moved other Medicaid programs: more predictable budgets and slower cost growth. Under fee-for-service, the state pays providers for each service delivered, so spending rises with use. Most managed care arrangements instead pay a plan a fixed monthly amount per enrollee, called a capitation rate, and the plan takes on the financial risk of covering everyone’s services within it. That should give the state a predictable cost per person and gives the plan a reason to manage care efficiently, through care coordination, shifting services from institutions to community settings, negotiating provider rates. Critics worry the savings can also come from people getting less: plans may approve fewer services, pay less for what they approve, or leave providers with rates so low they deliver fewer hours than authorized.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: What the spending data shows before any model
text:
What the spending data shows before any model

Adopting states started all over the map, but most ended up spending less per enrollee than they had before, even as typical states kept spending more.
Before adoption, these seven states don’t look alike. Arizona and Michigan spent well below the typical range, North Carolina tracked the median, and Kansas and Iowa spent far above it. What they share is what happens next. In Michigan, Wisconsin, North Carolina and Iowa, spending per enrollee in the I/DD category drops around the adoption year and stays down while the grey band keeps climbing, so the gap widens over time. Michigan falls by roughly half right after 1998 and stays flat for two decades.
The timing presents some challenges. In North Carolina, Kansas and Iowa, spending starts falling several years before the adoption year marked here. That could be states preparing for the switch, for example by restructuring waivers or tightening rates ahead of it, or it could mean the coded year is late. It also matters that Kansas, Iowa and North Carolina were spending well above typical states at their peaks, and unusually high spending tends to drift back toward the middle on its own. Those early declines are why the event study below checks for pre-existing trends.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: Spending fell after adoption, and kept falling
text:
Spending fell after adoption, and kept falling

Spending per enrollee in the I/DD category fell as soon as states adopted managed care, kept falling for about a decade, and never recovered.
Compared with states that never adopted, adopters’ spending dropped by about $324 in the adoption year and kept falling, to about $1,033 below never-adopters ten or more years later. Averaged over all post-adoption years, the drop is $728 per enrollee. Two cautions: past about seven years, the estimates rest on Michigan and Wisconsin alone, and adopters’ spending was already drifting down relative to other states in the years before adoption. “How much should you trust this?” tests whether that earlier drift could explain the drop.






Figure 3: Change in I/DD-category spending per enrollee relative to the year before adoption, with 95% confidence intervals

section: The drop is spending, not more enrollees
text:
The drop is spending, not more enrollees

The per-enrollee expenditures are not better explained by changes in enrollment which remained fairly steady in adopting states.






Figure 4: Log I/DD-category spending and log Medicaid enrollment around adoption

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: The money didn’t move to other Medicaid services
text:
The money didn’t move to other Medicaid services

Cutting spending in one part of Medicaid can push costs somewhere else, either because services get recorded under a different category or because cuts in one service raise demand for others, such as fewer home supports leading to more hospital or nursing home care. If that were happening, other categories would rise to offset the I/DD drop. They don’t. The categories that rose add up to about $192, none of them by a clearly measurable amount, and prescription drugs actually fell slightly. Total spending per enrollee on personal health care fell by $632, about 87% of the $724 drop in the I/DD category. Nearly all of the change comes from that category.
One shift this can’t rule out: these categories cover spending on services only. Any part of a capitated payment that a plan keeps for administration or margin falls outside them entirely.






Figure 5: Effect of adoption on Medicaid spending per enrollee, by service category

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
section: How much should you trust this?
text:
How much should you trust this?

Adopters’ spending was already drifting down before adoption: in this window it falls from about $197 above its pre-adoption level seven years out to zero, roughly $33 a year. That could reflect states preparing for the switch, such as restructuring waivers or holding down rates beforehand, or high spenders drifting back toward the middle. But the drift can’t account for what happens at adoption. Holding the comparison to the same five states throughout (Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, North Carolina and Wisconsin), spending drops $312 in the first year alone, about ten times the yearly drift. By year three it is $549 below its pre-adoption level, where the earlier drift alone would have predicted about $131. Averaged over the four post-adoption years, the drop is $443.

Same states, same window







Figure 6: Event study restricted to a balanced window





Could this happen by chance?

With only six adopting states, the usual standard errors aren’t reliable, so I checked the result another way: assign the same adoption years to randomly chosen states and see how big an “effect” shows up by chance. I did this 1000 times. None of the random assignments produced a drop as large as the real one (p < 0.001). That makes chance an unlikely explanation, though on its own it can’t rule out adopters differing from other states in some other way.






Figure 7: The actual estimate against 1,000 placebo adoption assignments









NoteWhy randomization inference?






Standard errors clustered by state assume there are many independent groups to learn from. Here only six states ever change treatment status, so clustered standard errors tend to be too small and confidence intervals too narrow. Randomization inference sidesteps that problem.
The procedure: take the six real adoption years, shuffle them, and assign them to six states drawn at random from the 50 states and DC (Arizona excluded, since it adopted before the data begin). Re-estimate the two-way fixed effects model on this fake assignment and record the estimate. Repeating this 1000 times builds the distribution of estimates you’d see if adoption had no effect anywhere. The p-value is the share of placebo estimates at least as large in absolute value as the real one.
Two limits. First, it assumes any state could plausibly have been an adopter; if adopters were systematically different, the comparison is less clean. Second, it tests the simpler two-way fixed effects estimate rather than the Sun–Abraham event study, and it doesn’t address the pre-adoption drift. That’s what the balanced-window check is for.

title: What Happened to I/DD Spending When States Moved to Managed Care?
text:
What this can’t tell us

This analysis shows that spending fell. It can’t show whether quality of care changed with it. The limited evidence on experience is mixed: people with I/DD in Illinois managed care described problems with access and navigating the system (Gibbons, Owen, & Heller, 2016), and some family caregivers in four managed-care states reported less flexibility and harder access to services (Williamson et al., 2016). Nor can this data separate lower prices from fewer services: spending can fall because care costs less or because less of it is delivered.
The data also misses money that never reaches services. CMS’s personal health care figures exclude administrative costs, including what managed care plans keep for administration and margin. Before drawing policy conclusions, a state would want to confirm that those costs are small enough not to cancel out the savings in service spending.
